title: Of cruelty
hook: Montaigne hated cruelty, even to animals (Essays 2.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Of Books. Your line was read for joy. Did you set down something dull, or read a page just because you wanted to? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

A thin, high cry from the edge of a field: a hare, caught in the dogs' teeth. Montaigne calls the chase a violent pleasure. And in the very same breath, he says he can hardly bear to hear that cry. The same chase, the same dogs, and a man who can't quite enjoy the ending. He doesn't resolve the tension. He just tells the truth about both. That honesty sets the tone of his essay called Of Cruelty.
screen: `A CRY AT THE EDGE OF A FIELD.` → `THE CHASE, A VIOLENT PLEASURE.` → `HE COULDN'T BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: First, the vice he hates most. Among all the vices, Montaigne writes, he cruelly hates cruelty, by nature and by judgment, as the extreme of them all. Notice the joke: he hates it cruelly. The one harshness he allows himself is toward cruelty itself. Second, the small creatures. He says he can't watch a chicken's neck being wrung without discomfort. He can't stand the hare's cry. And he admits, a bit sheepishly, that his nature is so tender that when his dog offers him a game at the wrong moment, he can't say no. Third, the courts and the wars. Even in justice, he says, anything beyond plain execution seems to him pure cruelty. And he says his own time is full of shocking examples, because of the lawlessness of the civil wars: people tormenting others for nothing more than the pleasure of watching. He saw it near home, and he names it. Fourth, the wider duty. He says there's a kind of respect, a general duty of humanity, that ties us not only to animals, which have life and feeling, but even to trees and plants. We owe justice to people, he says, and kindness and gentleness to other creatures that can receive it. He doesn't turn this into a rulebook. He doesn't tell anyone what to eat or whether to hunt. He just draws one line, around unnecessary pain. On an ordinary Tuesday, no cruelty starts small: the spider, the dog, the tone of voice.
screen: `THE EXTREME OF ALL VICES.` · `A CHICKEN, A HARE, A DOG.` · `NOTHING BEYOND PLAIN DEATH.` · `A DUTY TO ALL THAT LIVES.` · then, large: `NO CRUELTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with a creature. Sit, and let the breath slow. If there's an animal near you, a pet, a bird outside, a fly on the window, watch it for a while. If not, bring one to mind. Notice that it has life and feeling, as Montaigne put it. Let your attention be soft on it. Then choose one gentle thing to do for a creature today. Carry the spider outside. Fill the water bowl. Say yes to the dog's game, even at a bad moment. The bell holds the time.
Of cruelty. Montaigne hated cruelty above every vice, and said we owe kindness and gentleness even to animals, and some respect to trees and plants. Today's word.
Your line: no cruelty. Today, notice one small chance to cause less pain, to a person or a creature, and take it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Cruelty as a short, practical ethic: refuse needless pain, toward people first, and extend gentleness to animals and living things.

fork.setup: you're Montaigne, busy at your desk, and your dog drops a toy at your feet and looks up. what do you do?
options: send the dog away; you're working.
fork.reveal: he admits his nature is so tender that he can't refuse his dog a game, even when it's offered at the wrong moment.

original.note: French, from Of Cruelty: I cruelly hate cruelty.

trapdoor: what you thought: Of Cruelty is about being nice to animals.
what it means: needless pain is, for Montaigne, the worst vice of all, toward people first, and toward any creature that can feel.
what a scholar hears: the essay opens on virtue and natural goodness, and he says his own gentleness is more temperament than hard-won virtue. he claims no credit for it.
recall: a try, a test, an attempt

notes: The outline hook says Montaigne's hatred of cruelty to animals was 'unusual for his time'. The essay doesn't say this directly, so the script leaves it out (claims rule). Suggest the index hook be softened.
All Montaigne is paraphrased. The French 'je hais cruellement la cruauté' is from memory of 'Je hais, entre autres vices, cruellement la cruauté'; confirm.
The script avoids any position on hunting or diet, describing only what Montaigne says.

Editor pass: 2.11 calls the chase a violent pleasure but does not say he loved hunting; hook, screen and myth item now say only that. Cut the unsupported aside that he wrote about war and death 'without flinching'.
